course.chapter_intro: Chapter {n} of Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition (Sweigart, 2025), renewed for an advanced course.

playground.label: First program (uses input)
playground.code:
print('What is your name?')
my_name = input()
print(f'It is good to meet you, {my_name}.')
my_age = int(input('What is your age? '))
print(f'You will be {my_age + 1} in a year.')

findings: Chapter 1 of the 3rd edition introduces the interactive shell, expressions and their operators with precedence, the integer, floating-point and string data types, string concatenation and replication, variables, and a first program using print, input, len, str, int and float; it closes on how computers store data in binary.

Where the book stays practical, the reference documentation states what an advanced student should know underneath: Python integers have unlimited precision, while floating-point numbers are usually implemented as C doubles and carry the representation limits the tutorial documents; the Language Reference tabulates operator precedence from most to least binding; and PEP 8 fixes the naming conventions the book's variable examples follow informally.

For an advanced course, chapter 1 is best taught as the bridge from the book's basics to the Python students will actually run: the 3.13+ interpreter, f-strings rather than concatenation, precision and representation as real behaviour rather than trivia, and a first look at the ecosystem - uv for packages, and the free-threaded build as the preview of the course's multithreading outcome.

The Python in students' hands has moved since the book: Python 3.14 is the current bugfix release, first released on 2025-10-07, with 3.13 also in bugfix and 3.15's first release scheduled for 2026-10-01. Python 3.13 brought a better interactive interpreter, improved error messages, an experimental free-threaded build and an experimental just-in-time compiler. PEP 701 gave f-strings a formal grammar, making them the natural successor to building strings by concatenation. In the ecosystem, uv - a Python package manager built in Rust - was the most admired technology tag in the 2025 Stack Overflow survey, at 74 per cent.
title: Python basics for an advanced course

nodes.label: Value
nodes.body: Every Python expression reduces to a value, and every value has a data type that decides what can be done with it (Sweigart, 2025). Chapter 1 works with three, in its section The Integer, Floating-Point, and String Data Types: integers, floating-point numbers and strings (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Numeric value
nodes.body: Integers and floating-point numbers look alike in the shell but are stored differently: integers exactly, floats in binary with a fixed precision (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Integer
nodes.body: A Python integer has unlimited precision, so 2 ** 100 evaluates exactly to 1267650600228229401496703205376 rather than overflowing as in many languages (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A whole number. Python integers have unlimited precision, so 2 ** 100 is exact.

nodes.label: Floating point
nodes.body: Floats are stored in binary, so some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly: 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004, and round(0.1 + 0.2, 2) gives 0.3 - the reason behind the chapter's closing section, How Computers Store Data with Binary Numbers (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A number with a fractional part, stored in binary, so some decimal values cannot be represented exactly.

nodes.label: Text value
nodes.body: Text is a value like any other, and the chapter treats strings with the same expression rules it uses for numbers (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: String
nodes.body: A string is a sequence of characters between quotes, and the same operators that act on numbers act on strings with a different meaning (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A sequence of characters written between quotes.

nodes.label: Operation
nodes.body: Operators combine values into new values, and the rules for which operator applies first are fixed by the language, not by the reader (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Arithmetic operation
nodes.body: The chapter introduces seven arithmetic operators - +, -, *, /, //, % and ** - evaluated in a documented order (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Precedence
nodes.body: Operator precedence decides the result: 2 + 3 * 6 evaluates to 20, while (2 + 3) * 6 evaluates to 30, because ** binds first, then *, /, // and %, then + and -, and parentheses override the order (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The order in which operators apply: ** first, then *, /, //, %, then + and -; parentheses override it.

nodes.label: Integer division
nodes.body: Floor division and the modulus operator split a division into its whole part and its remainder: 23 // 7 is 3 and 23 % 7 is 2, while 23 / 7 gives the float 3.2857142857142856 (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Floor division gives the whole-number quotient; the modulus operator gives the remainder.

nodes.label: Text operation
nodes.body: Two operators work on strings: + joins them and * repeats them, which the chapter calls string concatenation and replication (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Concatenation
nodes.body: String concatenation joins two strings with +, so 'Alice' + 'Bob' gives 'AliceBob'; joining a string to a number raises a TypeError, because Python does not convert types silently (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Joining two strings with +. Joining a string to a number raises a TypeError.

error.out: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

nodes.label: Replication
nodes.body: String replication repeats a string with an integer, so 'Alice' * 3 gives 'AliceAliceAlice' (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Repeating a string an integer number of times with *.

nodes.label: Binding operation
nodes.body: Assignment is the operation that gives a value a name, so later expressions can use it (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Assignment
nodes.body: An assignment statement stores a value in a variable with the = operator, as the chapter's section Storing Values in Variables shows; PEP 8 recommends lower_case names with underscores for variables (Van Rossum et al., 2001).
nodes.definition: Storing a value in a variable with =; the variable names the value, and the name follows PEP 8's lower_case convention.

nodes.label: Built-in function
nodes.body: Chapter 1's first program uses six built-in functions - print, input, len, str, int and float - which are always available without importing anything; the sections Your First Program and Dissecting the Program walk through them line by line (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Input-output function
nodes.body: Two built-in functions connect a program to its user: print sends text out, and input reads text in (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Output
nodes.body: The print function writes its arguments to the screen as text, which is how the first program says hello (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: print() writes its arguments as text to the screen.

nodes.label: Input
nodes.body: The input function waits for the user to type and always returns a string, so a number typed at the keyboard arrives as text - the chapter's point about input as text (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: input() waits for the user to type and always returns a string - input as text.

nodes.label: Conversion function
nodes.body: Because input returns text, programs convert values between types with str, int and float (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Type conversion
nodes.body: The conversion functions change a value's type, so int('42') gives 42 and str(29) gives '29'; int('4.2') raises a ValueError because the text is not a whole number (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: str(), int() and float() convert a value between types; int() refuses a string that is not a whole number.

error.out: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '4.2'

nodes.label: Measurement function
nodes.body: Some built-in functions measure a value rather than convert it, and len is the first the chapter uses (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Length
nodes.body: The len function returns the number of characters in a string, so len('hello') is 5 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: len() returns the number of characters in a string.

nodes.label: Execution environment
nodes.body: Where code runs matters as much as what it says, and the Python students run in 2026 is newer than the one the chapter describes: 3.14 is the current release and 3.15 arrives on 1 October 2026 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Interactive environment
nodes.body: The chapter starts with Entering Expressions into the Interactive Shell, where each expression is evaluated as soon as it is entered (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Interactive shell
nodes.body: Python 3.13 replaced the interactive shell with a better interactive interpreter and improved its error messages, which changes what students see from their first expression (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The shell that evaluates expressions as they are typed. Python 3.13 replaced it with a better interactive interpreter.

nodes.label: Interpreter build
nodes.body: CPython is built in more than one way, and the build decides how programs can use the machine (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Free-threaded build
nodes.body: Python 3.13 introduced an experimental free-threaded build of CPython and an experimental just-in-time compiler, which previews the course's multithreading outcome (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A build of CPython, experimental since 3.13, that can run threads in parallel - the preview of the course's multithreading outcome.

nodes.label: Modern practice
nodes.body: An advanced course teaches the current idiom alongside the book's basics, so the chapter's string building and first program are paired with today's tools (Galindo Salgado et al., 2022).

nodes.label: String formatting
nodes.body: Building strings by concatenation works, but formatted string literals are the idiomatic way to mix text and values (Galindo Salgado et al., 2022).

nodes.label: F-string
nodes.body: An f-string evaluates expressions inside braces as it builds the string, so f'{2 ** 8}' gives '256'; PEP 701 gave f-strings a formal grammar for Python 3.12 (Galindo Salgado et al., 2022).
nodes.definition: An f-string evaluates expressions inside braces as it builds the string; PEP 701 gave f-strings a formal grammar.

nodes.label: Tooling
nodes.body: A Python programmer works through tools as much as through the language, starting with how packages and interpreters are installed (Stack Overflow, 2025).

nodes.label: Package manager
nodes.body: uv installs Python packages and interpreters; built in Rust, it was the most admired technology in the 2025 Stack Overflow survey at 74 per cent, and it installed the Python 3.14.4 used to check this chapter's examples (Stack Overflow, 2025).
nodes.definition: A tool that installs Python packages and interpreters. uv, built in Rust, was the most admired technology in the 2025 Stack Overflow survey.
